title: Kansas Could Hold the Cheapest Hydrogen on Earth. No One Can Get It Out Yet
description:
What if one of the cheapest clean energy sources in the world is sitting under Kansas, and nobody knows yet how to get it out?

On part two of this live Keystone Session, Brendan Bream breaks down geologic hydrogen. This is hydrogen that forms naturally underground, and it is quickly becoming one of the most closely watched exploration plays in energy. Pulling it straight from the ground could cost about half as much as making hydrogen from natural gas, and that process also releases CO2. Venture capital is pouring in, more than 100 companies are chasing it, and Kansas has become a global hotspot for exploration. Yet only one place in the world actually produces geologic hydrogen today: a field in Mali that was discovered by accident while drilling a water well.

Bream draws on his background in the oil and gas industry to separate the hype from the physics. He explains why Kansas has geologic success but not yet economic success, and why the hydrogen found so far is dissolved in salt water rather than sitting in a free-flowing pocket of gas. He also places the whole industry on the Gartner hype cycle: cresting the peak of inflated expectations and likely heading into the trough of disillusionment.

title: Banks Only Have 3 Credit Moves. Are You Using the Right One?
description:
Every bank has a long menu of products. For credit, though, Rickey Leathers says there are only three moves. Change the name, add a feature, and it’s still a credit card, a line of credit, or a term loan. The trick is knowing which one fits what you’re paying for.

On the last part of this Keystone Session, Rickey breaks down each of those three options and when to use them. He explains how the SBA and community lenders make capital easier to reach for small businesses. In an open Q&A, he takes on the questions owners actually bring him: business credit “hacks,” using an SBA 7(a) loan to buy an existing company, and whether a grant can count toward your down payment.

title: 14,600 Bridge Strikes a Year: The Repair That Beats Replacement
description:
Every year, an average of 14,600 vehicles collide with bridges across the U.S.: trucks clipping girders, overheight loads tearing into overpasses. When it happens on U.S. Highway 60 in Springfield, Missouri, the damage cascaded from the first girder to the second to the third, and the highway closed. The standard answer is to replace the bridge. Mohammed Abdel-Aziz's answer is: not necessarily.

This is part 2 of Abdel-Aziz's Session here at Keystone. As the director of the Structural Engineering Lab at the University of Missouri-Kansas City, his team is building and full-scale testing repair strategies for two of the most common ways bridges fail: corrosion and impact, before those repairs ever reach a real structure.

The first is corrosion repair. Steel bridge piles that have lost significant thickness underwater get wrapped in a fiber-reinforced polymer tube filled with concrete, essentially a structural Band-Aid. Abdel-Aziz's team validates the design computationally first, using Ansys LS-DYNA simulation, then proves it physically under full axial load in the SEL. The result: no measurable loss in the repaired section, with all damage pushed safely outside the repair zone. Some of these repairs use ultra-high-performance concrete (UHPC) reinforced with steel, basalt, or glass-fiber microfibers, designed to bridge cracks and reinforce the one thing plain concrete is bad at: tension.

The second is impact repair. Abdel-Aziz's lab runs full-scale crash tests on AASHTO Type II bridge girders to classify real-world impact damage and design a fiber-reinforced polymer or UHPC repair that restores a girder's strength without full replacement. The tests run for seconds; each one takes months of computational modeling to set up correctly. The same modeling approach also opens the door to real-time structural health monitoring, predicting how much strength a damaged column or girder has actually lost, so a repair can be sized to the real damage instead of over-engineered for a worst case that isn't there.

None of this happens in isolation. Abdel-Aziz frames the SEL as a hub connecting research, industry, and education with partners including Geiger, Western Form, and Ferroglobe in Kansas City, and material and research partners reaching Penn State, Michigan, Florida, Texas, and Virginia. Graduate and undergraduate students test alongside him, present at ACI and ASCE conferences, and take AISC-sponsored field trips, training that's meant to close the gap between classroom theory and what actually holds up a bridge.

title: The Ogallala Is Running Out. Two Kansas Counties Found a Way to Slow It.
description:
What happens to a region whose entire economy runs on water that won't come back for 300 years?

On part 3 of 3 of our Keystone Sessions talk, our representative of the Kansas Geological Survey lays out the reality of the High Plains (Ogallala) Aquifer in western Kansas. In some counties, 60 to 70 percent of the aquifer is already gone. Recharge from rainfall is about half an inch a year, so the region is effectively mining its groundwater. The driver isn't drought. It's pumping: in some counties, irrigation accounts for 97 percent of all water use.

The talk walks through the Survey's "estimated usable lifetime" map, which shows some areas with roughly 25 years left before wells can't sustain a center pivot. It then weighs the fixes people propose, from a Missouri River aqueduct to railing water west to treating oilfield produced water. Finally, it turns to the one approach already working: farmers in Wichita and Sheridan counties who voluntarily cut their pumping and stabilized their water levels.

title: How Scientists Map Water You Can't See: Helicopters, Blue Chalk, and a 500-Foot Tape
description:
Every year, Kansas can pump about seven million acre-feet of water for irrigation. That's roughly 70% of all the water the state uses, and much of it comes from underground.

On part 1 of 3 of this live Keystone Session, a presenter from the Kansas Geological Survey explains how groundwater works and why it matters across the western U.S. The first part of the story is geography. Because of the Rocky Mountain rain shadow, rainfall drops from nearly 40 inches a year in Kansas City to about 18 at the Colorado line. That shift turns at the 100th meridian, near Dodge City, where the state goes from a surface-water economy in the east to one that runs almost entirely on aquifers in the west. Some western counties have no reservoirs and no streams. Every drop they use comes out of the ground.

The talk covers who uses that water: cities, power plants, wildlife refuges, irrigation, and a livestock industry with twice as many cattle as there are people in the state. It also explains the prior appropriation rule that decides who gets water when supplies run short. Under that rule, the oldest permit wins, no matter what the water is used for.

Then comes the hard part: measuring something no one can see. That includes decades of drillers' logs, a helicopter towing a 60-foot antenna to create a CAT-scan-style map of the High Plains Aquifer, and water levels still checked by hand with a 500-foot steel tape coated in blue chalk.

title: Why Banks Say No: What Lenders Actually Look For in a Business Loan
description:
You’d never hand a stranger $100 without asking how and when you’d get it back. So why do so many business owners walk into a bank without answering that same question?

This is part two of three of this Keystone Session and today Rickey Leathers breaks down what loan readiness really means, drawing on years of coaching hundreds of small business owners through the lending process. Most of those owners describe getting a bank loan the same way: hurdles and hoops. Rickey argues the process makes more sense once you see it from the lender’s side. The single most common mistake he sees is a business owner who builds detailed projections for growth and forgets to include the loan payment itself.

title: Kansas Oil Peaked in the ’70s. Geologic Hydrogen Could Be Its Next Energy Boom
description:
What if the next energy resource in Kansas isn’t oil or gas, but hydrogen that has been building up underground the whole time?

Today we bring you part one of three of this live Keystone Session where Brendan Bream, a geologist with the Kansas Geological Survey and roughly 20 years in the energy industry, explains why Kansas may be sitting on an energy opportunity few people saw coming. His career took him from ExxonMobil to a faculty post at Vanderbilt and to helicopter-supplied drilling sites in the mountains of Papua New Guinea. He came to Kansas expecting a quiet job teaching the next generation of geologists, since the state’s oil production had peaked back in the ’60s and ’70s. Then geologic hydrogen came up.

Bream describes how the Kansas Geological Survey works. It is the second-largest state geological survey in the country, it turns every state dollar into about three federal research dollars, and it has put a team of former oil and gas scientists to work on a new question: is there usable hydrogen under Kansas, and could the state’s salt deposits store hydrogen like a battery?

title: The Hidden HIPAA Trap in Healthcare AI Agents
description:
What happens when a founder builds a healthcare AI agent before checking whether it touches protected health information and finds out too late?

In this Keystone Sessions talk, Gwen Gillette breaks down the compliance framework that determines whether an AI agent in healthcare needs a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) at all and why most builders get the order of operations backwards. Instead of starting with a tool, Gwen walks through HIPAA's Treatment, Payment, and Operations (TPO) framework as the first filter for any healthcare AI project, then digs into what actually counts as de-identified data (it's not just stripping names; ZIP codes, the 18 required fields, and time-shifting all matter), and why "payment" is still the least-solved corner of healthcare AI.

The core of the talk is a side-by-side build: two AI agents from the same practice one flagging prior authorization denials (requires a BAA, touches PHI, needs a permanent human sign-off) and one identifying the slowest-paying insurers (no PHI, no BAA, runs almost anywhere). Gwen makes the case for which one a practice should actually build first, and why speed-to-value and regulatory exposure often point in opposite directions.

If you're building, deploying, or evaluating AI agents in a regulated industry, this is a working model for scoping compliance before you write a line of code.

title: The 5-Second Rule That Can Stop a Bad Financial Decision
description:
Most people don't ignore their bank balance because they're bad with money, they ignore it because money is emotional. In this Keystone Sessions talk, Miriah breaks down why financial stress hits young adults transitioning to independence especially hard, and shares practical tools to build confidence one small decision at a time.

Miriah's work focuses on financial literacy for young people aging out of foster care, but the tools she shares, from decision-making frameworks to reframing financial setbacks, apply to anyone navigating money stress and building independence for the first time.

title: Inside the High Plains Aquifer: Where Kansas Gets Its Water, and Why It's Getting Harder to Reach
description:
Where does Kansas's water actually come from, and why is it getting harder to reach?

On part 2 of 3 of this live Keystone Session, our representative of the Kansas Geological Survey takes us underground into the two aquifer systems that supply most of the state's water, and the field work it takes to monitor them. That work includes snow drifts, landowners, and a frozen possum blocking a well. The first system is the Kansas River alluvial aquifer, a fast-reacting system that moves almost in lockstep with the river above it. The second is the High Plains Aquifer, the largest groundwater supply in Kansas and one of the largest in the country, stretching from South Dakota to Texas. It took millions of years to fill. In parts of western Kansas, the water table now sits 400 feet down and drops a little further every year.

The most uncomfortable finding may be the simplest one: the biggest threat to Kansas's groundwater isn't Oklahoma or anyone else downstream. It's what Kansas does with the water itself.
